claims.claim: The web part only accepts a form, saves a file and shows a results page. Each of those takes milliseconds in Python
claims.measured: python-flask plaintext 1,732 req/s on 1 CPU, about 0.6 ms of CPU per request; p50 35.55 ms at 64 connections (gthread variant 14.72 ms)
claims.why: Measured per-request cost in Flask is under a millisecond to tens of milliseconds under load, which fits 'milliseconds' and is tiny next to a 20–90 s simulation.

claims.claim: Rewriting the web layer in Go, Rust or Node ... wouldn't make anything faster
claims.about: Go / Rust / Node vs Python Flask web layer
claims.measured: Plaintext: go-gin 53,941, rust-actix 86,102, node-fastify 40,730 vs python-flask 1,732 req/s
claims.why: Those servers measured 20–50× faster per request, but the claim is about end-to-end job time, which depends on the simulation, and the simulation isn't benchmarked.

claims.claim: A Flask app fits your load easily (20 users, a few dozen runs a day)
claims.measured: python-flask 1,732 req/s plaintext, 1,529 req/s for a single DB row, on 1 CPU
claims.why: Even the slowest Flask setup handles over a thousand requests per second per core, far more than a few dozen jobs a day need.

claims.claim: A 90-second request will tie up the web server
claims.measured: I/O wait test (10 ms per request): python-flask 276 req/s, p50 915 ms; flask-gthread 374 req/s, p50 678 ms
claims.why: Sync Flask throughput collapsed and latency rose sharply when each request held a worker for only 10 ms, so holding one for 90 s would clearly block it.

claims.claim: Python threads won't run NumPy code in parallel here
claims.why: The benchmarks use single-CPU containers and pure-Python fib, so they don't measure NumPy running in parallel threads.

claims.claim: FastAPI: its async model doesn't help CPU-heavy work ... No real gain
claims.measured: CPU fib(20): python-fastapi 1,257 req/s vs python-flask 1,078 and flask-gthread 1,149 req/s
claims.why: On the CPU-bound test FastAPI was only about 10–15% faster than Flask, which supports 'no real gain'.
